cases.description: The title is empty.
The description is blank.
The description is longer than the 155 characters a search result shows.
The publication date is 30 February.
The slug has capital letters and spaces.
The piece has no category.
The same category is listed twice.
A category is not in the closed vocabulary.
The piece is tagged funding but has no beat.
The author name is blank.
The author is a person, not the Desk.
The opening paragraph is shorter than the length the rule requires.
There are two key takeaways, not three to five.
The body is shorter than the length the rule requires.
A sentence is padded until the piece is over 850 words.
All the paragraphs sit under one heading.
A section heading ends in a question mark.
A section heading runs to more than 80 characters.
A section of the piece has the heading of the notes that the Desk writes itself, "What we couldn't verify".
A section heading is blank.
A claim that needs a limitation is left out of the limitation sentence that describes its group.
The 'What we couldn't verify' section is missing from a piece that rests on a company's own claims.
A fact sentence is added that cites no claim at all.
A sentence cites a claim, c-99, that is not in the piece.
A sentence states a number whose digits are swapped from the number of the claim it cites.
A sentence gives the number of the claim it cites with a different unit.
A sentence gives a number written in words, with its unit, that is not the number of the claim it cites.
A sentence states an amount in a word, such as "twice", that no claim can support.
A sentence gives a date that is not the date of the claim it cites.
A sentence names a company that no claim it cites mentions.
A sentence gives a date as a word that mixes letters and digits, "mid-2027", that no claim it cites contains.
A section heading states a figure, as in "the company ships 500 arms".
A section heading contains a quoted passage.
A section heading names a company, Harlow Logistics, that no claim of its section mentions.
A claim lists a value that is not in the quotation it says it was taken from.
A claim lists the value 2, which is only the end of the 12 in its quotation, and the sentences that cite it give a delivery time of 2 weeks.
A sentence puts words in quotation marks that the cited source never said.
A quotation changes one word of the passage it quotes.
A claim that comes only from another outlet is stated as plain fact, with no attribution.
A sentence is marked attributed to a tier-2 outlet but never says which outlet.
An analysis sentence rests on another outlet's reporting.
A claim that rests only on another outlet is given the basis of a primary source, a filing.
A claim from a primary source is given the basis reported, which is for what another outlet reports.
The title is the Desk's own analysis.
Analysis sentences are added until they make up more of the body than the rule allows.
An analysis sentence works out a percentage that no fact sentence states.
An analysis sentence opens with a company, Harlow, that no fact sentence mentions.
An analysis sentence starts with a lowercase name, harlow, so the rule for the opening word cannot read it.
An analysis sentence brings in a company, Harlow Logistics, that no fact sentence mentions.
A limitation sentence is placed in a body paragraph instead of 'What we couldn't verify'.
A limitation sentence cites a claim, c-99, that is not in the piece.
One limitation sentence covers claims that have different bases.
One limitation sentence covers more claims than the rule allows, though its wording is the template wording.
One limitation sentence covers claims that two different outlets reported.
A limitation sentence is reworded to say the figures were independently confirmed.
A limitation sentence keeps its text but is labelled with the wrong template.
The slug is the slug of a piece that is already published.
The title repeats a recent title with only a stop word changed.
A takeaway calls the shipment a 'game-changer'.
A section heading says 'revolutionary'.
